scenarios.title: Connect the branch with a network route
scenarios.summary: Build the missing router entry, choose its neighboring next hop, and verify traffic and replies.
scenarios.objective: Client must reach Server at 10.40.1.20 through R1 and R2. Add a static network route on R1 for 10.40.1.0/24 using its directly connected R2 neighbor. Keep the supplied addresses and forwarding on R1/R2. Verify the complete trip and reply; a default or single-host workaround does not meet this network-route task.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.

guide.title: Inspect attached networks
guide.why: R1 already reaches the office and the transit link, but not the remote branch.
guide.action: Choose R1. Compare Addresses & interfaces with Connected networks and route rules.

guide.title: Build and verify the route
guide.why: A network entry must direct branch traffic to a reachable router neighbor.
guide.action: Choose Static routes, add the requested /24 row, then Check configuration. Open applied paths if either direction fails.

scenarios.explanation: R1 knows its connected office and transit networks. A static 10.40.1.0/24 entry via R2’s 10.0.0.2 on transit supplies the missing direction. R2 already has the reverse office route, and Server has a default to R2. The route’s exact distance can vary when no equally specific candidate competes; the prefix, usable immediate next hop and resulting endpoint behavior matter.
hints: Follow the cable from R1’s transit interface to R2. Which neighboring address is on that same /30?
On R1, add destination 10.40.1.0/24. The outgoing interface is transit; the next hop belongs to R2, not Server.
scenarios.simplifications: Native configuration fields model bounded IPv4 static forwarding; they are not Cisco IOS or Linux command syntax. Only private/documentation endpoints, conventional /1–/30 interfaces, /0–/32 route prefixes and immediate on-link next hops. No real packets, ARP cache, dynamic routing, ECMP, recursive next hops, ACL/NAT or timing. Supplied interface up/down is operational state; a two-ended failure sets both ends. A missing neighbor alone does not withdraw an eligible static route. Return paths must work. Official sources checked 2026-10-22; this is partial current CCNA v1.1 practice, not full exam/equipment preparation.

concepts.title: Routes are directions
concepts.text: A device first checks its attached networks. For a different network, a static route supplies directions you configure: the destination network, outgoing interface and next-hop neighbor. A /24 network route serves that whole address block, not just one computer.

concepts.title: Choose the neighbor, not the final server
concepts.text: The next hop must be the neighboring router’s address on your outgoing cable. R1 cannot directly use a distant server as its next hop. In the editor, Add static route creates a draft row; replace its default /0 if the task asks for a specific network.

concepts.title: Verify both journeys
concepts.text: Check configuration applies all valid drafts together, then checks the requested endpoints and their replies. Inspect applied forwarding paths shows where a trip stops. Connected networks are derived from up interfaces; route distance defaults to 1 for static entries.

ipv4_routing_teaching.example_description: A separate topology uses Client 172.20.10.10 and Server 172.22.1.20. R1 has no route to the branch. Load example settings to inspect a working 172.22.1.0/24 route via neighboring R2, then Apply and test example.

outcomes.label: Client reaches Server and receives a reply

ipv4_routing_teaching.try_change: Change only the example route distance from 1 to 25, then test. With no competing route for that prefix it still works. Change its next hop to the distant server and test the specific diagnostic.

scenarios.title: Repair the journey back
scenarios.summary: Diagnose a delivered request whose reply cannot find the office.
scenarios.objective: Client requests reach Server, but no reply returns. Diagnose the applied path and restore a static network route on R2 for the office 192.168.10.0/24 through its R1 neighbor. Keep all supplied addresses, forwarding and the working forward path. Verify that Client receives a reply; a route only to one office host is insufficient.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.

guide.title: Find where the reply stops
guide.why: The applied trace identifies the failing direction instead of assuming every failure starts at the client.
guide.action: Open Inspect applied forwarding paths; read the reply failure. Inspect the named router’s static entries.

guide.title: Restore office-wide replies
guide.why: A route to the network supports the stated office, unlike a one-host patch.
guide.action: On R2 add the office /24 through its directly connected R1 neighbor, then check the complete configuration.

scenarios.explanation: Server already sends replies to R2. R2 has only its branch and transit connected networks, so it needs 192.168.10.0/24 via 10.0.0.1 on transit. That restores the return trip without changing the working forward route. A /32 patch can reach this one client but does not satisfy the explicitly requested network entry.
hints: The forward trip already reaches Server. Read the reply failure before editing Client.
R2 needs the office network as its destination; its immediate neighbor toward that network is R1 on transit.

concepts.title: Reachable is a round trip
concepts.text: Getting to a server is only half the task. The server sends a reply toward the original source, and every router on that return trip needs suitable directions too.

concepts.title: Read the first failure
concepts.text: Inspect applied forwarding paths distinguishes forward delivery from a failed reply. Follow the reply toward the office and find the first device missing that network route; changing a working client default cannot supply a missing entry on a different router.

ipv4_routing_teaching.example_description: The separate practice uses office 172.20.10.0/24. Requests arrive at Server 172.22.1.20; R2 lacks directions back. Load the example route on R2, apply, and compare the forward and reply paths.

outcomes.label: Client reaches Server and receives a reply

ipv4_routing_teaching.try_change: Replace the example /24 return route with 172.20.10.10/32. The single client may receive replies, but the requested office-network requirement fails. Restore the /24.

scenarios.title: Repair the more-specific detour
scenarios.summary: Keep a working default while repairing the network entry that overrides it.
scenarios.objective: Client reaches Sibling at 10.40.2.20, but Server at 10.40.1.20 takes a dead end through Spare. Repair R1’s static 10.40.1.0/24 entry so it serves Server through R2. Keep a default entry serving Sibling, keep all addresses and R1/R2 forwarding, and verify both endpoints. Do not replace the assignment with individual host routes.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.
steps: Repair one direction without losing the other

guide.title: Compare destination matches
guide.why: Both default and /24 match Server, but their prefix lengths differ.
guide.action: On R1 inspect both route rows and identify the more-specific one. Inspect the path stopping at Spare.

guide.title: Repair one direction without losing the other
guide.why: Changing distance alone cannot make a matching /24 defer to /0.
guide.action: Edit the /24’s next hop and outgoing interface toward R2, keep the default serving Sibling, then check both endpoints.

scenarios.explanation: The 10.40.1.0/24 entry matches Server more specifically than 0.0.0.0/0, even at distance80 or150. Its old direction led to Spare, which had no onward route. Pointing that network entry to 10.0.0.2 on transit restores Server. Sibling continues using the default. Distance becomes decisive only among equally specific eligible choices.
hints: Compare which row matches Server most specifically. Its distance need not be smaller than the default’s.
The /24 row must use R2’s transit next hop; leave the working default for Sibling.

concepts.title: More detail wins first
concepts.text: A route for a smaller address block is more specific: /24 names 256 addresses, while /0 is the default for anything else. For a matching destination, /24 wins before distance is considered.

concepts.title: Distance compares equally specific choices
concepts.text: A higher distance on a /24 does not make a matching /0 take over. Repair the network entry’s direction rather than trying to make its distance larger. Here Spare is a real neighbor but has no onward branch path.

concepts.title: Keep an unaffected service working
concepts.text: Troubleshooting must restore the broken path without losing a working one. This task checks the repaired network entry and the default entry actually serving the sibling network.

ipv4_routing_teaching.example_description: In the separate practice, the default via R2 reaches 172.22.2.20, but a 172.22.1.0/24 row sends 172.22.1.20 to Spare. Load and apply the repaired network direction, then inspect both paths.

outcomes.label: Client reaches Server and receives a reply
Client reaches Sibling and receives a reply

ipv4_routing_teaching.try_change: Keep the working /24 direction but change its distance to 150. It still beats the default for that subnet. Then point the /24 back at Spare with distance 1; only that subnet fails.

scenarios.title: Send one host through a different router
scenarios.summary: Use a host route for a special endpoint without redirecting its neighbors.
scenarios.objective: Server at 10.40.1.20 needs an intentional exception through Spare: R1 must use backup for that one address. Peer at 10.40.1.30 must keep using R1’s network route through transit and R2. Add a static /32 host route on R1 for Server, preserve the /24 serving Peer, all supplied addresses and router forwarding, and verify Client’s full Server trip and reply.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.

guide.title: Identify the exception’s scope
guide.why: A broad direction would change neighbors that must keep their existing path.
guide.action: Compare Server and Peer. Choose a route prefix that matches only Server.

guide.title: Verify both hosts
guide.why: The special path and unchanged normal path are separate outcomes.
guide.action: Add the /32 via Spare on R1, then check. Inspect Server and Peer forward paths and Client’s reply.

scenarios.explanation: R1’s 10.40.1.20/32 via 10.0.0.6 on backup matches only Server and wins over its /24, regardless of the /32’s higher distance. Peer keeps the /24 via R2. Server may reply through R2; both journeys work without requiring symmetric paths. /32 host routes are supported here while /31-/32 interface assignments remain excluded.
hints: A whole /24 includes Peer as well as Server. Which routing prefix matches exactly one address?
On R1 add 10.40.1.20/32 via Spare’s neighbor address on backup. Preserve the existing /24 via R2.

concepts.title: One address can have its own direction
concepts.text: A /32 route matches exactly one IPv4 address. It can override a broader network entry for that host while leaving its neighbors on the normal path. This is a routing prefix, not a /32 interface assignment.

concepts.title: A deliberate exception is different from a broken detour
concepts.text: Both branch routers can reach the server network here. The task intentionally sends one host through Spare. Its return trip may use a different valid router. A successful reply does not need to follow exactly the same path back. A check sent by R1 uses its chosen outgoing interface’s address as the source, unlike a Client check. The supplied R2 route back to R1’s reserve subnet lets that router-origin reply return too.

ipv4_routing_teaching.example_description: The practice sends only 172.22.1.20 through Spare, while 172.22.1.30 stays on the normal network route. Load the /32 example and compare the two applied forward paths.

ipv4_routing_teaching.try_change: Change the example exception destination from 172.22.1.20/32 to 172.22.1.0/24. Both rows then have the same specificity; distance can redirect the peer or hide the intended exception, and the explicit host-route task no longer passes.

scenarios.title: Restore the primary and floating backup
scenarios.summary: Choose between equal prefixes and prove the backup after an operational withdrawal.
scenarios.objective: R1 should normally reach Server through transit, using backup only when both primary transit interfaces on R1 and R2 are down. Repair the two static routes for 10.40.1.0/24 so the primary is preferred and the floating backup remains usable. Keep all addresses and router forwarding. Check configuration tests normal operation and a separate copy with both primary transit interfaces down, including Client’s reply path.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.

guide.title: Restore normal preference
guide.why: The backup is taking normal traffic because its equally specific candidate has lower distance.
guide.action: On R1 compare the two /24 entries. Give transit the preferred distance without disabling backup.

guide.title: Prove the failure path
guide.why: A backup that never carries a tested trip is only a saved row, not a verified repair.
guide.action: Check configuration. Inspect both the normal and primary-down outcomes, including the reply path through R2.

scenarios.explanation: Both R1 entries name 10.40.1.0/24, so their distances decide preference: a lower eligible transit distance wins normally. When the controlled case brings both transit ends down, those connected and static candidates are unavailable; the backup direction and R2’s backup return route carry traffic. A missing neighbor alone does not withdraw an otherwise eligible route. Many unequal distance pairs from1–254 are valid.
hints: Compare distances only after confirming both rows have exactly the same destination prefix.
Choose a smaller distance for transit than backup, keep both entries eligible, then read the controlled failure outcomes.

concepts.title: Choose between equal destination blocks
concepts.text: When two eligible entries name the same prefix, lower administrative distance is preferred. It is a preference value, not latency or hop count. Equal distinct paths are outside this model; distance255 is ineligible.

concepts.title: A floating route waits for withdrawal
concepts.text: A less-preferred static entry can become usable when the preferred outgoing interface is down. The checked failure sets both primary ends down in a copy, so your saved configuration stays unchanged. Keep a working return path during that failure too.

concepts.title: A silent neighbor is not route withdrawal
concepts.text: An otherwise eligible static entry does not disappear just because its next-hop neighbor is absent. The backup is not a health monitor. This unit does not model tracking, dynamic protocols or automatic carrier detection.

ipv4_routing_teaching.example_description: The practice has two routes for 172.22.1.0/24, but the reserve currently has lower distance. Load the corrected preference and test both normal and controlled primary-down cases.

scenarios.title: Complete the resilient branch handover
scenarios.summary: Bring a new desk online, diagnose route and forwarding faults, and prove normal and backup service.
scenarios.objective:
Bring Client2 onto office 192.168.10.0/24 with a different usable address from Client (192.168.10.10) and R1 (192.168.10.1). Keep every supplied address elsewhere.

Both office clients must reach Server and receive replies. R1 must normally use transit for the branch 10.40.1.0/24 and use backup when both primary transit ends are down. R2 must normally return to the office through transit, with backup available for failure. Diagnose forwarding, next-hop and return-route faults; keep R1/R2 able to forward.

Use the address and static-route editors, then Check configuration. It verifies both clients in normal and tests with both primary transit interfaces down. Do not disable the reserve or patch only one client’s return route.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the first failed outcome with the current addresses and selected route. Fix that cause, then check again; a successful forward trip still needs a working reply.
steps: Repair routers and verify the handover

guide.title: Prepare the new desk
guide.why: A blank, occupied or reserved address cannot support an ordinary workstation.
guide.action: Assign Client2 a free office host address with /24; keep every supplied address elsewhere.

guide.title: Repair routers and verify the handover
guide.why: Normal traffic, both clients’ replies and a tested reserve path are all required.
guide.action: Inspect R1 forwarding and next-hop/distance choices, then R2 return paths. Check all normal and primary-down cases and retry the first remaining failure.

scenarios.explanation: A valid handover gives Client2 any unoccupied usable 192.168.10.x/24 address, enables R1/R2 forwarding, sends the branch /24 through the actual R2 neighbor on transit with a lower distance than backup, and restores office-wide return directions. The controlled two-ended transit failure then uses backup in both directions. All specified endpoint assignments remain fixed; one successful client or one normal-state probe is insufficient.
hints: Inspect Client2 first, then R1 forwarding and route eligibility. A route pointing at R1’s own address is not a path to R2.

After normal transit works, inspect R2’s office return routes and the controlled primary-down outcomes. Keep an eligible backup and an office /24 return route; a single-host patch does not cover the office network.

concepts.title: Work from a handover checklist
concepts.text: This assignment combines earlier skills: choose a free host address, preserve working addresses, enable router forwarding, use neighboring next hops and verify both return paths. Fix one cause at a time; partial results help you keep what already works.

concepts.title: Inspect saved rows and selected behavior
concepts.text: A saved route can be ineligible, or eligible without being chosen. A next hop assigned to the same router is not a neighboring router. After edits, Check configuration applies valid drafts and tests the full handover in normal and primary-down states.
